note: Extracted 13 September 2026. A separate record from CJC-1295 for the same reason TB-500 is separate from thymosin beta-4: the name practitioner sources and sellers use for it — "CJC-1295 without DAC" — belongs chemically to a different molecule. Sources: the practitioner handbooks (SRC-001 Seeds, SRC-002 Peptide Handbook, SRC-003 Campbell, SRC-004 cheat sheet, SRC-005 Hack Smith), two analyses of seized products (SRC-071 Norway, SRC-072 Denmark) and the CJC-1295 originator paper for contrast (SRC-066). The PubMed ledger for both names is the CJC-1295 screen; no human study of this peptide was identified in it. Seeds, the Peptide Handbook, the cheat sheet and Hack Smith are cited by file page; Campbell by the book's page numbers. Amounts appear only in protocol fields.

compound.shortDescription: A 29-amino-acid, short-acting version of growth-hormone-releasing hormone, sold and described as "CJC-1295 without DAC". Widely used according to practitioner books; no study in people identified.
compound.simpleSummary:
Modified GRF (1-29) is a lab-made copy of the first 29 building blocks of the hormone that tells the pituitary gland to release growth hormone, with a few changes that make it last longer than the natural version — minutes rather than seconds, according to handbooks.

**It is usually sold under someone else's name.** Handbooks and sellers call it "CJC-1295 without DAC". In the scientific literature, CJC-1295 is a different, long-acting molecule. When a product sold as CJC-1295 was tested, it turned out to be this shorter peptide.

**No study in people was found.** Everything this index holds about how it is used comes from practitioner books, which describe nightly injections, often combined with another peptide called ipamorelin. Their claims about how long it lasts in the body could not be traced to a measurement. Seized products have also been found to contain slightly altered versions of it.
compound.practitionerSummary: Modified GRF (1-29) is described by practitioner sources as a tetrasubstituted 29-residue C-terminally amidated GHRH(1-29) analogue (Tyr-D-Ala2 …), the core peptide of CJC-1295 without the added maleimidopropionamide lysine, and therefore without covalent albumin binding. Handbooks give its half-life as about 30 minutes against 5-7 minutes for native GRF(1-29); no primary pharmacokinetic study was identified. Mass spectrometry of a preparation seized in Norway and sold as CJC-1295 found a 29-residue amide consistent with this peptide, and powders seized in Denmark contained N-terminally glycine-extended modified GRF 1-29 analogues. No human or animal administration study of this molecule specifically was identified in the screen. Practitioner regimens are nightly or multiple-daily subcutaneous injections, commonly combined with ipamorelin; none cites a study.
compound.unknownsSummary: Not established: any human pharmacokinetics, including the half-life every handbook repeats; any effect on GH, IGF-I or outcomes in people; safety; the combination with ipamorelin; and what purchased products labelled with this name or with CJC-1295 contain, given seized products with altered sequences.

compound.molecularDescription: 29-residue C-terminally amidated GHRH(1-29) analogue with four substitutions, as stated by practitioner sources; lower-case a denotes D-alanine.
compound.nomenclatureNote: This record exists because of a naming problem. "CJC-1295 without DAC" suggests CJC-1295 with a component removed. Chemically it is the 29-residue core; the originator's CJC-1295 is that core plus a reactive lysine. A product sold simply as "CJC-1295" was found to be this peptide. Evidence about CJC-1295, including its human trials, is not evidence about this molecule.

claims.claimText: Practitioner sources describe modified GRF (1-29) as a 29-residue amidated GHRH analogue beginning Tyr-D-Ala, and identify it as CJC-1295 without DAC; the originator describes CJC-1295 as a tetrasubstituted hGRF(1-29) with an added reactive lysine, so the peptide these sources describe lacks the albumin-binding group that defines CJC-1295.
claims.plainLanguageText: Modified GRF (1-29) is the shorter peptide inside CJC-1295, without the hook that makes CJC-1295 long-acting.
claims.interpretationNotes: The comparison of the two descriptions is this index's reading; neither source makes it explicitly.
claims.uncertaintyText: The handbook sequence has not been checked against an analytical reference for this peptide.

disagreements.plainLanguageText: Handbooks and sellers call it 'CJC-1295 without DAC'. The scientists who made CJC-1295 defined it as a longer molecule with a hook this peptide does not have.
disagreements.explanationNotes: The market name implies one molecule in two versions. Chemically they are two molecules: the originator's CJC-1295 is this 29-residue core plus a reactive lysine.
disagreements.resolutionBasis: The originator abstract (SRC-066) defines CJC-1295 by the added maleimidopropionamide lysine; practitioner sources describe this peptide as the 29-residue amide without it; a seized product sold as CJC-1295 (SRC-071) was the 29-residue amide. Two records are kept and no evidence crosses.
